stops.name: Fisher Building
stops.teaser: A 30-story art deco tower with a roof that glows gold at night.
stops.map: Fisher Building, 3011 W Grand Blvd, Detroit, MI
stops.clue: Go to the New Center area, north of downtown, and find the tall tower with the green roof on West Grand Boulevard.
stops.safety: West Grand Boulevard is busy. Use crosswalks. Respect the building's lobby hours and rules.

q.hint: More than a couple of dozen, fewer than forty.

story: The Fisher Building was completed in 1928. Albert Kahn Associates designed it, with Joseph Nathaniel French as chief architect. It has 30 stories. The roof is 428 feet up and the spire reaches 444 feet.

The Fisher family paid for it with money from selling Fisher Body to General Motors. The three-story barrel-vaulted lobby uses forty kinds of marble and was decorated by the Hungarian artist Géza Maróti. Several sculptors worked on the outside, including Corrado Parducci.

The roof was first covered in gold-leaf tiles. They were covered with asphalt during World War II and replaced with green tiles. Since the 1980s, colored lights have made the green tiles look gold at night. It became a National Historic Landmark on June 29, 1989.
stops.fact: The lobby uses forty kinds of marble.
stops.disputed: "Detroit's largest art object" is a nickname that the Detroit News used. Wikipedia treats it as a quote, not a measured fact.

claims.t: The Fisher Building was completed in 1928.
The Fisher Building's roof has always been green.
claims.why: It was gold-leaf tiles at first, then green after World War II. The lights make it look gold at night.

spot.q: At night colored lights make the Fisher Building's roof tiles look gold. What color are the tiles?
spot.why: The gold-leaf tiles were covered with asphalt during World War II and replaced with green tiles. Since the 1980s, colored lights have made them look gold at night.

story: After the Great Fire of 1805, Judge Augustus Woodward planned the rebuilding of Detroit around Campus Martius. It is named for the main square in Marietta, Ohio, the first capital of the Northwest Territory. The name is Latin for Field of Mars.
Detroit's coordinate system starts here, marked by a medallion in the stone walkway. Seven Mile Road is seven miles north, Eight Mile Road is eight miles north, and so on.
The new park was dedicated on November 19, 2004. It has a seasonal ice rink designed to look like Rockefeller Center's rink, but larger. A Civil War-era monument stands on Campus Martius.
stops.fact: Seven Mile and Eight Mile Roads are named for their distance from here.
stops.disputed: Wikipedia lists the park as created in 1850 and 2004 without explaining 1850. Treat any single founding year with caution.

claims.t: Detroit's coordinate system starts at Campus Martius.
claims.why: Wikipedia: the Point of Origin medallion marks the start.

claims.t: Eight Mile Road is named for its distance to Lake Michigan.
claims.why: It is eight miles north of the Point of Origin.

sources.t: Detroit Historical Society: Campus Martius Park

spot.q: Detroit's coordinate system starts at Campus Martius. How far north of it is Eight Mile Road?
spot.why: Seven Mile Road is seven miles north, Eight Mile Road is eight miles north, and so on.

stops.name: Historic Fort Wayne
stops.teaser: A stone fort built to face Canada, which never fired a shot at it.
stops.clue: Go to Historic Fort Wayne on the Detroit River and find the long limestone barracks. The fort is mainly open for tours on summer weekends, so check before you go.
stops.safety: Check opening times and rules before you go.
stops.field: Field notes pending: nobody has walked this stop for the app yet.

q.hint: Count the rows of windows, then look under the roof.
q.verify: Wikipedia describes a 3½-story limestone barracks. Count the floors on site. Written from sources, not yet checked on site.

now.head: Today
now.label: The barracks, 2008

story: Congress paid for a chain of forts in 1841, and Detroit's was meant to answer Fort Malden, across the river in Canada. Building began in 1842, and the fort was finished in 1851 at a cost of $150,000.
The barracks is a 3½-story limestone building in five sections, each meant to house one company of soldiers. It dates from 1848. Brick washrooms and kitchens were added to the back in 1861.

The two countries settled their differences before any cannon was installed, and the fort sat nearly empty for about a decade with a single watchman. In the Civil War it mustered Michigan volunteers, and in World War II it became a huge motor supply depot. Since 1948 the Army has handed it to the City of Detroit in pieces.
stops.fact: The fort sat nearly empty for about a decade with one watchman.
stops.disputed: Wikipedia dates construction to 1842-1851. The Detroit Historical Society says the Army surveyed the site in 1840 and finished the fort by 1850. Both give 1848 for the barracks.

claims.t: Fort Wayne's cannons defended Detroit in battle.
claims.why: Wikipedia says the countries settled their differences before any cannon was installed, with no sign the intended artillery was ever put in.

claims.t: Michigan volunteer soldiers were mustered at Fort Wayne in the Civil War.
claims.why: Wikipedia and the Detroit Historical Society both describe it as a mustering post for Michigan regiments.

spot.q: In 1861, what was added to the back of the Fort Wayne barracks?
spot.why: Wikipedia says brick washrooms and kitchens were added to the rear of the barracks in 1861.

stops.name: Michigan Central Station
stops.teaser: A skyscraper train station that sat empty for 30 years, then came back.
stops.map: Michigan Central Station, 2001 15th St, Detroit, MI
stops.clue: Go to Corktown, southwest of downtown, and look for the tall tower with rows of big windows beside the old rail yard.
stops.safety: Be respectful of the active campus. View from public sidewalks, watch traffic and do not enter closed areas.
stops.field: Field notes pending: nobody has walked this stop for the app yet.

q.hint: More than a dozen, fewer than twenty.

story: Michigan Central Station opened in December 1913. Warren & Wetmore and Reed & Stem designed it. Allen Stem of Reed & Stem also helped design New York's Grand Central. The tower is 18 stories with more than 500 offices.
The last train left in 1988. After that the building sat vacant for about 30 years.
Ford bought it from the Moroun family in 2018 and reopened the station in June 2024 as part of a campus project that cost $950 million.
stops.fact: Allen Stem also designed Grand Central.
stops.disputed: Some stories call it a sad ruin forever. It was reopened, so be careful with old photos that show the empty building.

claims.t: The station has been in continuous use since 1913.
claims.why: The last train left in 1988 and the building sat vacant for about 30 years.

spot.q: Michigan Central Station sat vacant for about 30 years after its last train in 1988. Who reopened it in June 2024?
spot.why: Ford bought it from the Moroun family in 2018 and reopened it in June 2024 as part of a $950 million campus project.
